slides.title: Errors in Transmission - Why They Happen?
slides.body:
The Noise Problem
When bits travel across a physical medium - a copper wire, a WiFi signal, a fibre optic cable - they are exposed to noise, interference, and signal degradation. This can flip bits: a 0 becomes a 1, or a 1 becomes a 0

The Data Link Layer's job is to detect these errors before the corrupted data reaches the Network Layer. It does this by adding redundant information to each frame - extra bits that allow the receiver to check whether any bits were flipped during transmission

slides.title: Checksum - Sum-Based Error Detection
slides.body:
How TCP/IP Detects Errors
Checksum is the error detection method used by TCP, UDP, and IP headers. It is more powerful than simple parity because it considers the content of the entire data block, not just the count of 1s

slides.title: Checksum - Sum-Based Error Detection
slides.body:
Divide the data into fixed-size segments (e.g., 16-bit blocks)
Add all segments together using one's complement arithmetic
Take the one's complement of the result  this is the  checksum 
Append the checksum to the data and transmit
How Checksum Works (Sender Side)

slides.title: Checksum - Sum-Based Error Detection
slides.body:
How Checksum Works (Receiver Side)
Divide the received data (including checksum) into the same fixed-size segments
Add all segments together (including the checksum) using one's complement arithmetic
If the result is all 1s (1111...1111) → No error detected. If the result is not all 1s → Error detected

slides.title: CRC - The Most Powerful Error Detection
slides.body:
Introduction
CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) is the most widely used and powerful error detection method in the Data Link Layer. It is used in Ethernet (IEEE 802.3), WiFi (IEEE 802.11), USB, and many other protocols

slides.title: CRC - The Most Powerful Error Detection
slides.body:
Introduction
Core Idea
Treat the data as a binary polynomial. Divide it by a pre-agreed generator polynomial. The remainder of this division is the CRC - appended to the frame as a Frame Check Sequence (FCS)

slides.title: CRC - The Most Powerful Error Detection
slides.body:
Both sender and receiver agree on a Generator Polynomial (e.g., x3 + x + 1 → binary: 1011)
Append (n-1) zeros to the data, where n = number of bits in generator
Divide the augmented data by the generator using modulo-2 division (XOR division - no borrows or carries)
CRC Process - Sender

slides.title: CRC - The Most Powerful Error Detection
slides.body:
CRC Process - Sender
The remainder of this division is the CRC value. Replace the appended zeros with this CRC

slides.title: CRC - The Most Powerful Error Detection
slides.body:
CRC Process - Receiver
Divide the received frame (data + CRC) by the same generator polynomial using modulo-2 division
If remainder = 0 → No error. If remainder ≠ 0 → Error detected

slides.title: Hamming Code - Detecting and Correcting Errors
slides.body:
From Detection to Correction
Error detection tells the receiver that something went wrong. Error correction goes further - it identifies exactly which bit was corrupted and fixes it without needing a retransmission
Hamming Code (developed by Richard Hamming, 1950) is the most fundamental error-correcting code. It can:
Detect up to 2-bit errors
Correct single-bit errors automatically

slides.title: Hamming Code - Detecting and Correcting Errors
slides.body:
Introduction
Hamming Code inserts parity bits at positions that are powers of 2: Position 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...
These parity bits each cover a specific subset of data bits. Together, their values form a binary number that points to the exact position of the error

slides.title: Hamming Code - Detecting and Correcting Errors
slides.body:
How Many Parity Bits Required?
For m data bits: find r such that 2r ≥ m + r + 1
4 data bits → r = 3 parity bits needed. Total bits transmitted = 4 + 3 = 7 (Hamming(7,4))

slides.title: Hamming Code - Detecting and Correcting Errors
Hamming(7,4) Example
slides.body:
Computing parity bits (even parity)
p1 (position 1)
Covers positions 1, 3, 5, 7 → bits: p1, d1, d2, d4 = p1, 1, 0, 1. Count of 1s (excluding p1) = 2 (even), so p1 = 0
p2 (position 2)
Covers positions 2, 3, 6, 7 → bits: p2, d1, d3, d4 = p2, 1, 1, 1. Count = 3 (odd) → p2 = 1
p3 (position 4)
Covers positions 4, 5, 6, 7 → bits: p3, d2, d3, d4 = p3, 0, 1, 1. Count = 2 (even) → p3 = 0

slides.title: Hamming Code - Detecting and Correcting Errors
slides.body:
Error Detection and Correction at Receiver
Receiver recalculates all parity bits from the received frame. Each recalculation produces a 0 (parity OK) or 1 (parity error). These results form a binary number called the syndrome

slides.title: Hamming Code - Detecting and Correcting Errors
slides.body:
Error Detection and Correction at Receiver
No error
Syndrome = 000
The syndrome value (in binary) gives the exact position of the corrupted bit
Syndrome ≠ 000
error corrected
Receiver flips that bit
Syndrome = 011 (binary) = position 3 → bit at position 3 is corrupted. Flip it → original data recovered

slides.title: Data Link Control - Managing the Communication
slides.body:
DLC Components
After handling framing and error detection, the Data Link Layer must also manage how two directly connected nodes communicate - when to send, how fast to send, and what to do when things go wrong. This is called Data Link Control (DLC)

slides.title: Data Link Control - Managing the Communication
slides.body:
Three DLC components
01
Controls which device can transmit at a time
ENQ/ACK
Sender asks permission (ENQ), receiver confirms (ACK), then data is sent
Poll/Select:
A primary device controls communication - polls devices to receive and selects them to send

slides.title: Data Link Control - Managing the Communication
slides.body:
02
Prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver
The receiver has a buffer (limited memory). If the sender sends faster than the receiver can process, the buffer overflows and data is lost
Flow control mechanisms slow down the sender to match the receiver's capacity
Two main protocols: Stop-and-Wait, Sliding Window 
Three DLC components

slides.title: Data Link Control - Managing the Communication
slides.body:
Three DLC components
03
Handles detected errors - 
ensures data is retransmitted when frames are corrupted or lost
Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) - receiver detects error using CRC → sends NAK (Negative Acknowledgement) or simply does not ACK → sender retransmits
Go-Back-N ARQ and Selective Repeat ARQ are advanced variants (part of Sliding Window)

slides.title: Stop-and-Wait - One Frame at a Time
slides.body:
Introduction
Stop-and-Wait is the simplest flow control and error control protocol. The sender sends one frame, then stops and waits for an acknowledgement (ACK) before sending the next frame

slides.title: Stop-and-Wait - One Frame at a Time
slides.body:
How Stop-and-Wait Works?
Sender transmits Frame 0
Sender stops - waits for ACK from receiver
Receiver receives Frame 0, checks CRC. If correct → sends ACK 1 (ready for frame 1)
Sender receives ACK 1 → sends Frame 1. Then waits again

slides.title: Stop-and-Wait - One Frame at a Time
slides.body:
Error Case
If receiver detects error (CRC fails) → sends NAK (or no ACK). Sender has a timer - if it expires without an ACK → retransmit the same frame
Lost ACK
 If the ACK itself is lost  sender times out and retransmits Frame 0. Receiver may get a duplicate. Sequence numbers (0 and 1 alternating) allow the receiver to detect duplicates
How Stop-and-Wait Works?

slides.title: Sliding Window - Keeping the Pipe Full
slides.body:
Multiple Frames In-Flight at Once
The Sliding Window protocol solves the efficiency problem of Stop-and-Wait by allowing the sender to transmit multiple frames before waiting for an acknowledgement. The number of unacknowledged frames allowed at once is called the window size (W)

slides.title: Sliding Window - Keeping the Pipe Full
slides.body:
Multiple Frames In-Flight at Once
Sender Window:
← window slides right as ACKs arrive →
Window Size and Efficiency:
Efficiency = W / (1 + 2a), where a = Tprop / Tframe
If W ≥ 1 + 2a → Efficiency = 100% (sender never has to wait - pipe always full)
If W < 1 + 2a → Efficiency = W / (1 + 2a) - less than 100%

slides.title: Sliding Window - Keeping the Pipe Full
slides.body:
